sections.heading: Keep my life from making the gospel look ugly
sections.text: O God, please do not let my life become empty, useless, or harmful. Keep me from living in a way that gives people a reason to mock your truth. When I enjoy the freedom you have given me in Christ, do not let me twist it into an excuse for selfishness or sin. Teach me to use my freedom to love and serve people, not to indulge myself.
theological_themes: Christian freedom is not permission to sin but a call to loving service.
A believer’s conduct can either commend or dishonor the truth of the gospel.
The Christian life should be fruitful rather than spiritually empty.

scripture_references.connection: Paul directly connects Christian freedom with serving one another through love, warning believers not to use liberty as an opportunity for the flesh. This grounds the prayer’s concern that freedom in Christ be used for holiness and love rather than self-indulgence.

Paul urges believers, especially those who teach or represent the faith, to live with integrity so that opponents have no legitimate reason to speak evil. This supports the request that the pray-er’s life not bring reproach on the way of truth.

sections.heading: Make my faith beautiful in ordinary relationships
sections.text: Father, help me care not only about being technically right, but also about being gracious, wise, and good to be around. Teach me to seek what builds my neighbor up. Let my faith show itself in patience, kindness, humility, and steady love. Make my life with you both true and winsome, so that what I say about the gospel is backed up by the kind of person I am becoming.
theological_themes: Love for neighbor is a central expression of obedience to God.
Christian maturity includes both essential truth and the beauty of Christlike character.
The gospel should be made visible through conduct as well as words.

scripture_references.connection: Paul calls believers not to live merely to please themselves, but to seek their neighbor’s good and upbuilding. That is the heart of this section’s request for a faith that serves and strengthens others.

Paul directs the church to give attention to what is honorable, just, pure, lovely, commendable, and worthy of praise, and to practice what they have learned. This supports the prayer’s concern for what is not only doctrinally essential but also beautiful and commendable in Christian life.
Paul says faithful conduct can adorn the doctrine of God our Savior. This gives biblical shape to the request that the pray-er’s profession of faith be attractive rather than harsh or off-putting.

sections.heading: Let my whole life point people toward Jesus
sections.text: Lord Jesus, help me speak of your way not only with my words but with my tone, my reactions, my habits, and my choices. Let my life and my lips tell the same story. When I meet people along the road, give me courage and warmth to say, in whatever way is fitting, that I am heading toward the place you have promised, and that there is good for them in coming with me to you.
theological_themes: Witness includes both verbal testimony and embodied holiness.
Christians are pilgrims moving toward God’s promised future.
Evangelism is an invitation to share in the good God gives through Christ.

scripture_references.connection: Peter joins readiness to speak about hope with gentleness, respect, and a good conscience. This fits the prayer’s desire to bear witness to Jesus with both speech and manner of life.
Jesus teaches that visible good works should lead others to glorify the Father. This supports the request that the pray-er’s conduct, not only words, point people toward God.
Moses invites Hobab to come with Israel because the Lord has promised good to his people. The prayer echoes that pilgrim invitation: come with me toward the good God has promised.

sections.heading: Prepare me for this short and uncertain life
sections.text: Father, this life is brief, changeable, and not under my control. Prepare me for whatever you appoint for me. While I am here, make me useful. As I travel through this life, give me the comfort that comes from trusting you. And when the time comes for me to leave this world, carry me safely through death into the life you have promised.
theological_themes: Human life is brief and uncertain, so wisdom and readiness are needed.
God’s providence governs the believer’s circumstances.
The believer can face death with hope because life with Christ continues beyond the grave.

scripture_references.connection: James reminds believers that they do not control tomorrow and should live under the Lord’s will. This grounds the prayer’s sober acceptance of life’s uncertainty and dependence on God’s appointments.
Moses asks God to teach his people to number their days so they may gain wisdom. That supports the prayer’s desire to live usefully and wisely within a short life.
Paul views both living and dying in relation to Christ, with death bringing him to be with Christ. This illuminates the request for a safe passage out of this life and hope beyond death.

sections.heading: Make me useful, steady, and unashamed
sections.text: Make me, by your grace, refreshing where people are weary, preserving where things are decaying, and clear where there is darkness. Let the life of Christ in me overflow for the good of others. Keep me from being ashamed of Jesus or of his words. Do not let fear stop me from doing what I know is right, and do not let my weakness make me give up before I obey. Teach me to trust your strength more than my own.
theological_themes: Believers are called to be salt and light in the world.
Christian usefulness comes from God’s life and grace, not self-sufficiency.
Faithfulness requires courage when obedience is costly or weakness is felt.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus names his disciples the salt of the earth and the light of the world, tying their visible lives to the Father’s glory. This directly supports the prayer’s desire to have a preserving and illuminating presence in the world.
Jesus speaks of living water flowing from those who come to him, referring to the Spirit. This supports the request that the life God gives would overflow from the believer for the good of others.

Paul tells Timothy that God gives not fear but power, love, and self-control, and urges him not to be ashamed of testimony about the Lord. This closely fits the prayer’s plea for courage in known duty despite fear or weakness.

sections.heading: Use everything to make me ready for what is next
sections.text: God, teach me to see my life in your light. Shape my judgment so I can understand things truly, and shape my heart so that what I understand makes me more holy. Use your fatherly discipline, your providence, your Word, prayer, worship, and the life of your people to prepare me for the duties still ahead of me, for the serious hour when I must die, and for the joy and service that wait beyond the grave.
theological_themes: God gives wisdom and moral clarity by his light and Word.
Providential discipline is part of God’s fatherly work of holiness.
God uses ordinary means of grace to prepare believers for faithful life, death, and eternal service.

scripture_references.connection: The psalm confesses that true light is found in God’s light. This supports the request to see all things rightly because God himself gives the light by which reality is understood.

Hebrews describes God’s discipline as painful but purposeful, producing holiness and righteousness. This grounds the prayer’s desire that providential hardships would sanctify rather than embitter the believer.
Paul teaches that Scripture equips the person of God for every good work. This supports the request that God’s appointed means would prepare the pray-er for remaining duties.
John’s vision of the new creation includes God’s servants serving him in his presence. This gives biblical support to the prayer’s hope for joy and service beyond the grave.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The phrase about what is “ornamental as well as essential in religion” could sound like concern for mere religious appearance. I rendered it as the biblical beauty and winsomeness of Christlike character, while keeping the original concern that true religion should be commendable and inviting, not merely correct.

The original’s confidence that God prepares believers through “all the disciplines of providence” reflects a strong doctrine of providence that can be pastorally sensitive when applied to suffering. The adaptation keeps the idea of God’s fatherly use of hardship without implying that every painful event is easy to interpret.

The reference to preparation for death and what lies beyond assumes a historic Christian hope of conscious life with Christ and future service in God’s presence; this is preserved rather than softened.
significant_interpretive_choices: “A blot or a blank in life” was rendered as becoming harmful, empty, or useless, since the original seems to hold together both negative witness and fruitlessness.
“Hold forth the way of Jesus with my temper as well as my tongue” was interpreted as witness through tone, reactions, habits, and choices, not merely through evangelistic speech.
“The Lord’s given place” was treated as God’s promised destination for his people, with the prayer framed as a pilgrim invitation to others rather than a claim about any earthly location.
The images of dew, salt, light, and fountain were kept as concrete images but expressed in contemporary terms: refreshing, preserving, illuminating, and overflowing for others’ good.
